The folks at @juicebox_work looked at recruiter trends (outbound searches from recruiters) and are seeing exactly the same thing I saw:
1. Demand for software engineers is dropping
2. Demand for PMs is growing
3. AI engineering growing even faster
4. Design hiring down 20% YoY https://t.co/PFsokL4wVv

quote.text:
STATE OF THE TECH JOB MARKET IN 2026

Twice a year, I dig into trends in hiring and job openings. This is the fifth report I've done, and the most surprising yet:

1. PMs are winning in the AI era
2. Engineering demand has stalled
3. Design openings are at a record low
4. Every role now requires AI skills
5. Tech jobs are concentrating in the Bay Area
6. Remote roles are at a record low
7. The tech job market is growing fast, but mostly outside of software (gasp!)

Full report here:

items.summary: .@mona_sarantakos (Head of Product, @Muse): "I did not think shopping was gonna be as big of a use case as it's become." https://t.co/ABpCWd3Fje
items.body: .@mona_sarantakos (Head of Product, @Muse): "I did not think shopping was gonna be as big of a use case as it's become." https://t.co/ABpCWd3Fje

quote.text:
In late January, @natfriedman pinged a few people at @Meta. He’d been using OpenClaw, and told them they needed to try it.

Mona Sarantakos couldn’t find a Mac Mini, so she spent the weekend setting it up on a Raspberry Pi and gave it access to her email and calendar. Her husband told her, “That is so not safe.”

But by Monday morning, it had pulled together everything her kids had going on at school that week. She pinged Nat back: “This is it. I’m in.”

The team spent the next seven months building something safe and simple enough for everyone. They called it @Muse. It became the fastest-growing AI consumer product ever.

Mona is head of product for Muse and VP of product at Meta Superintelligence Labs. In her first podcast interview, she shares the inside story of how they built and launched Muse.

We discuss:
🔸 Why they waited seven months to launch, despite getting started before all of their competitors
🔸 The two levers that actually move activation for an AI agent
🔸 How @natfriedman, @alexandr_wang, and @finkd each left their imprint on the product
🔸 Why the Muse team relies on "agent swarms" more than dashboards
🔸 Why taste is now the most important PM skill

Listen now 👇

comments.text: Shopping makes sense in hindsight. One person holds the intent, the budget, and the final click, so the review step is free: you look at the cart before you pay. The hard version is buying for a team, where someone else approves and the agent has to show its work.
comments.text_zh: 事后看，购物这件事说得通。意图、预算和最后那一次点击都在同一个人手里，所以审查步骤是免费的：付钱前看一眼购物车就行。难的是给团队采购，审批在别人手里，智能体还得把过程讲清楚。

comments.text: shopping was always going to win. it is the one question where people already accept a recommendation from a stranger, so the trust bar is on the floor.
comments.text_zh: 购物注定会胜出。这是人们本来就愿意接受陌生人推荐的那类问题，信任门槛本来就低在地上。

comments.text: Same surprise on our side. We expected shoppers to use agents to find products faster. Most of what they ask is advice instead. Will this fit, does it go with what I bought last month, is it worth waiting for Black Friday.
comments.text_zh: 我们这边也一样意外。我们本以为购物者会用智能体更快地找商品。他们问得最多的却是建议。这个合身吗，和我上个月买的搭吗，值得等到黑五吗。

items.body:
The two biggest levers the @Muse team has found for activation:

1. Word of mouth. "Ads don't resonate until people see someone they relate to using it."

2. Solving the first prompt. “People freeze on the first prompt.” So they added idea starter packs. All you have to say is “Let’s do it.”

comments.text:
I mean this is really true for any AI chat box-based product wrt mass market adoption.

My personal fave sound bite was that an agent’s only useful if you can hand something over and stop worrying about it. Otherwise, you’re just managing more software.
comments.text_zh:
我是说，这对任何基于 AI 对话框、面向大众市场普及的产品都非常适用。

我个人最喜欢的一句是：智能体只有在你能把事情交出去、并且不必再操心时才有用。否则，你只是在管理更多软件。

comments.text: blank prompt = user does the product's job. starter packs flip it: product proposes, user says yes
